\begin{abstract}
Adoption of formal verification has long been hindered by the cost of manual specification.
To prove high-level properties, one must also write contracts for supporting functions, many of which are mechanical and low-level.
Specification inference automatically derives such contracts from the program.
We present a hybrid of mechanical and agentic inference for Move, a smart contract language, integrated into its verifier, the Move Prover.
A large language model (LLM) agent drives inference and verification through a tool that calls the Move Prover and derives specifications from code by weakest-precondition (\WP) analysis.
We evaluate our approach on 26 targets, 24 of them extracted from public Move functions of the Aptos framework that have no specifications, under a frontier model and a mid-tier model of the same family (Sol~5.6 and Terra~5.6).
With and without \WP, the agent completes over 90\% of its runs, so agentic inference is effective on its own.
Adding \WP\ lowers its cost by 11--21\% overall and by 40--64\% on targets without loops.

	\keywords{Specification inference \and Weakest precondition \and Reference elimination \and LLM agents \and Move Prover}
\end{abstract}

\subsubsection*{Data Availability Statement.}
The corpus is published with the inference plugin at~\Anon{\cite{MoveFlow}}{\cite{MoveFlowAnon}}: the package extracted from a pinned commit of the Aptos repository, the reference specifications, and the mutants.
The round archives behind every table and figure --- per-cell costs, token counters, wall times, and mutant outcomes --- and the scripts that produce them from the archives are published there as well; \Anon{\cite{SpecInferenceCorpus}}{\cite{MoveFlowAnon}} explains how to verify the corpus, re-score a round, and rerun the experiment.

\Section{Per-Target Results}
\label{sec:appendix}

Tables~\ref{tab:sol} and~\ref{tab:terra} give, for each target and tactic, the mean cost per cell over the four replicates, mean input/output tokens in thousands (I/O k), the hybrid mean cost as a percentage of agent-only (vs. agent), and whether the specification killed every withheld mutant in all four replicates (\Checkmark) or a mutant survived (\XSolidBrush, subscripted with the count where more than one replicate failed); $\circ$ marks an unmeasured cell.
Input counts include cached tokens.
The targets above the middle rule have no loop that needs an invariant.
